title: Leveraging High‐Resolution Topobathymetry to Assess Parsimonious Reach‐Scale Flood Inundation Mapping
content:
Abstract

Forecasting flood inundation requires accurate flood discharges, topography, and a means to map discharge to water level. In the continental United States, the National Water Model forecasts flooded areas using the Height Above Nearest Drainage—Flood Inundation Mapping (HAND-FIM) approach. HAND-FIM utilizes a Synthetic Rating Curve (SRC) and forecasted discharge to compute flood inundation within a river reach. Within the National Water Model, SRCs are currently developed using river segment-averaged geometry extracted from a 10-m Digital Elevation Model; however, high-resolution topography and hydrodynamic models allow the full complexity of channel morphology to be leveraged to assess the HAND-FIM approach. We utilize high-resolution topobathymetry coupled with satellite images across a range of flows and established rating curves to calibrate 2D hydraulic models for three reaches of the South Fork Eel River, California. To assess the impact of reach-scale hydraulic variability on SRCs, we construct an ensemble of rating curves based on high-resolution cross-stream elevation transects. We generate inundation extents using the ensemble of rating curves and HAND-SRCs and assess their performance against the calibrated model inundation extents. We find that a single rating curve can produce accurate reach-scale flood inundation, although it is not the rating curve that best represents reach-scale hydraulics. HAND-FIM performance improves when slope, roughness, and channel geometry within the SRC are corrected together, as correcting parameters individually can reduce performance. Improving the HAND-FIM approach has the potential to reduce uncertainty in flood prediction and provide advanced warning of flood extent across the United States.
